works.title: Capt. Glen claiming the prisoners after the burn- ing of Schenectady,
works.note: Catalogue text: " On the night of Feb. 9th, 1690, during a violent snow storm, a party of savages and French, dis- guised as Indians, commanded by Le Moyne de St. Helene, and d'Aillebout de Mantel, surprised and burnt Schenectady. On account of the kindness formerly shown by Capt. Glen and his family to certain French prisoners, brought in by the Mohawks during the Border forays, the offcers had orders to spare him, with his relations and property. Unable to prevent the slaughter, he had wit- nessed the confagration from his house, half-a-mile distant, expecting to be himself attacked. In the morning, however, being sent for by the French Commander, on receiving assurances of safety, he went over to the village, and denied relationship to none who asked his protection, so that the dizap- pointed Indians exclaimed,^ Every one seems to be a kinsman of Coudre's, (the Indian name of Capt. Glen.) About noon (Sunday) the enemy set off from Schenectady, tak:ng all the plunder they could carry away with them, including forty of the best horses. The rest, with all the cattle and other domes- tic animals, lay slaughtered in the street."

works.title: Angels bearing St.Cath- arine to Mount Sinai,
works.note: Catalogue text: " St. Catharine, Virgin and Martyr, disputed with fty heathen Philosophers, and converted them all to the true faith. * * *^ On account of which, the Emperor Maxentius caused her to be cast into prison, and an Engine invented to put her to a cruel death. She was tied to one of two wheels, armed with sharp spikes, and they laid their hands on the other to turn it about. when an angel from God brake the bands wherewith the Virgin was tied, and shie fell to the ground without any hurt. The same angel struck the wheels, which fell among the Pagans. and killed many of them. The Emperor immediately caused the youthful Christian to be beheaded ; but angels rescued her reimains, and conveyed them to Mount Sinai; where, in the ninth century, they were happily discovered, in an uncorrupted state. An order of Knights, fo; the protection of her sepulchre, wore white habits, in token of the spotless purity of thcir Patroness, ornamented with a half-wheel, armed with spikes, and traversed with a sword stained with blood."--See Lives of the Saints.

works.title: The Indian Hunter,
works.note: Catalogue text: Oh! why does the white man follow my path, Like the hound on the tiger's track ? Does the fush on my dark cheek waken his wrath ? Does he covet the bow of my back? He has rivers and seas, where the billows and breeze Bear riches for him alone ; And the sons of the wood never plunge in the food Which the white man calls his own. Then, why should he come to the streams where none But the red skin dare to swim ? Why, why should he wrong the hunter, one Who never did harm to him ?'--Eliza Cook. The Artist, C. P. Cranch.

works.title: THE MARRIAGE OF DOCTOR FRANCIS LE BARON AND MARY WILDER (Illustration)
works.note: Catalogue text: DOCTOR FRANCIS LeBARON. Plymouth was often without a physician. * * * In 1694 there was no surgeon there, and the wife of Goodman Hunter is said to have been in much suffering for want of one. A French privateer had just been wrecked in Buzzard’s Bay ; her accomplished surgeon, only twenty-six years old, was FRANCIS LeBARON, supposed to be the scion of some Huguenot family then in royal disfavor, and bearing an assumed name. While in Plymouth, on his way to Boston as a prisoner-of-war, he heard of Goodwife Hunter’s case and treated it with great success. The selectmen procured his release by Lieutenant-Governor Stoughton, and his settlement at Plymouth as their surgeon. He married Mary Wilder, of Hingham, September, 1695, and died nine years later, at Plymouth, where his quaint little head-stone on Burial Hill is now remarkable for its beautiful finish and preservation.—Goodwin’s Pilgrim Republic, Note, page 380. works.title: (C.) THE SNAKE DANCE (Illustration)
works.note: Marked "(C.)" before the subject in the catalogue: in competition for the Clarke prize (catalogue Memoranda, PDF p. 26). Catalogue text: “The Snake Dance” is a solemn bi-annual ceremony of the Moqui Indians of Arizona. It is the culminating rite in a series of ceremonies, and is the most remarkable survival of prehistoric nature worship extant. It is probably a petition for rain. The dance occurs at sunset in a plaza in the pueblo of Wal-pi, about seven hundred feet above the surrounding plain. The snake priests are the active participants; their bodies are stained with red and their faces are with black—the streamers of red buckskin typifying the snakes. The priests are divided into groups of three, the “Carrier,” who places one or more of the snakes between his lips when he is supposed to become at once blind; the “Hugger,” who supports him, endeavors with his whip to attract the snakes' attention, and the “Gatherer,” who walks behind and secures the snakes that may be dropped. At the end of the dance the snakes are liberated to bear the petitions to the Gods. Dimensions as printed in the catalogue's illustration caption: 84 x 144.

works.title: Honore de Balzac
works.note: Address as catalogued: a Gand. Statuette en cire exécutée d'après un portrait authentique fait d'après nature en 1837.  La seule version réelle d'un Balzac en ronde-bosse, la seule conforme au rapport de ceux qui l'on connu et a la science physiognomonique. Remarquez l'énormité du bassin, ces hanches et cette croupe de formidable commère, n'est-ce pas la sublime mère Gigogne, de la Comédie Humaine. Je signale l'importance de cette effigie a M. Rodin, qui doit faire un Balzac; il ne peut que copier Van Boosteront, pour rendre vraiment la physionomie de SA MAJESTIE L'EMPEREUR du Roman, le plus grand génie de ce siècle, après ou avec WAGNER    Wax statuette exécute after an authentic portrait made from life in 1837.  The only real version of a Balzac in the round, the only one that conforms to the report of those who knew him and to the science of physiognomics. Notice the enormity of the pelvis, those hips, and rump of formidable gossip. Isn't that the sublime Mother Nest from the Comédie Humaine? I would like to point out the importance of this effigy to M. Rodin, who is to make a Balzac; he can only copy Van Boosteront to render truly the physiognomy of His Majesty the Emperor of the Roman, the greatest genius of this century, after or with Wagner.

works.artist_dates: Born at Leiden in 1468; died at Leiden in 1533.
works.title: A Knight (Charles V) on Horseback
works.lender: Lent by The Worcester Art Museum.
works.note: The composition, especially that of the horse, is influenced by Dürer's engraving, Knight, Death and the Devil (1513). Dr. Janson pointed out that the figure on horseback probably represents Charles V and that the painting was executed soon after the Emperor's successful campaign in Tunis in 1535. This would preclude the likelihood that Engelbrechtsz, who died in 1533, is the author of the painting. While his deduction is convincing, his attribution to Jan Vermeyen is impossible for stylistic reasons. G. J. Hoogewerff is probably correct in giving the painting to Cornelis Cornelisz, the second son of Engelbrechtsz (1493-1544). (De Noord-Nederlandsche Schilderkunst, 1939, III, p. 204). The painting is closely related to Engelbrechtsz to whom it has been attributed by Friedländer and others, but shows a slight difference in style which can be explained by accepting an execution in Engelbrechtsz' workshop, which was taken over by Cornelis Cornelisz after his father's death. COLLECTIONS: Hilder; Crawford; Samuel Rogers; Earl of Northbrook. DESCRIBED: Friedländer, op. cit., X, No. 108; Horst W. Janson, Worcester Art Museum Annual, Vol. I, 1935-36, pp. 19-31.

Hoogewerff (op. cit., III, p. 352) who had not seen the original, as argument that the present painting and the group of paintings by the same master must be the work of Lucas Cornelisz. These paintings had formerly been attributed by Friedländer to Jan de Cock (Jan Wellens de Cock of Leiden; member of the Guild at Antwerp in 1503; died there about 1527). The basis of Friedländer's attribution was an engraving of about 1550 after a St. Christopher in the Bissing Collection, by our artist. This engraving is signed J. Kock C. Dankertz exc. and above these names is the word pictum. Beets and Hoogewerff believe these are the names of the editors and that the artist's name (before pictum) disappeared in the later states of the print, which are the only ones still in existence. In any case, the date and the close connection of this painting and others by the same artist with the atelier of Engelbrechtsz point to identification with Lucas Cornelisz. A painting in the Vienna museum (No. 652a) closely related to ours, is a partial copy after the Pieta in Engelbrechtsz's triptych in Leiden, which was executed about 1515-1520. The copy could hardly be earlier than 1520; this would coincide with the dates of Lucas Cornelisz but not with those of Jan Wellens de Cock, who at this time had lived in Antwerp for many years. Several small portraits also, one of which is signed with the name of Lucas Cornelisz and represents Sir Thomas Wyatt the Elder, correspond with the style of Engelbrechtsz who lived in England in later life.

works.title: George Washington (The "Port-hole" Portrait)
works.lender: Lent by The Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts, Philadelphia.
works.note: First president of the United States. When Peale painted this portrait in 1824, Washington had already become legendary. Peale created his likeness out of studies made when his father, Charles Willson Peale, had painted Washington nearly thirty years before. "I painted it," Peale said, "under the influence of extraordinary excitement and vivid recollection." And, as he had a good deal of P. T. Barnum in his nature, he immediately launched a campaign by lecture and pamphlet to have the new likeness accepted as the authentic national portrait in place of Stuart's "Athenaeum" head, which was then the favorite. As a made-up head, it cannot be accepted as a reliable portrait but its portrayal of Washington as a grandiose romantic hero shows how he appeared to the eyes of that time. It became very popular—by his own statement Peale painted seventy-nine replicas.

works.title: John Quincy Adams
works.lender: Lent by the City of Boston, Massachusetts.
works.note: Sixth president of the United States, painted about 1844-47. This portrait is also that of a flinty character—a courageous, intelligent, acid, self-righteous man who spent his life in the nation's service. After the close of his one term as President he was elected to Congress in 1831 and served there until his death, becoming a great single-handed defender of the right of petition against the slavery party. "Mr. Adams chose wisely and according to his constitution," wrote Emerson in his Journal (1843), "when, on leaving the Presidency, he went into Congress. He is no literary old gentleman, but a bruiser, and loved the melée . . . He is an old roué who cannot live on slops, but must have sulphuric acid in his tea." Dated 1845.

works.section: The People — II. Elegance and Romantic Beauty
works.note: Fanny Kemble belonged to a famous theatrical family which included her father Charles, her uncle John Kemble, and her aunt Mrs. Siddons. She came to the United States with her father in 1832. Her youth and beauty and the charm of her portrayal of Shakespeare's heroines were a national sensation. In spite of her talent she disliked the stage and although her marriage in 1834 with a Georgia planter, Pierce Butler, ended in divorce after a few years, she never returned to the stage. works.title: The Conspiracy of Pontiac Revealed to Major Gladwin at Detroit by an Indian Girl
works.lender: Lent by The Burton Historical Collection of the Detroit Public Library.
works.note: In the spring of 1763 Detroit alone of all the English forts west of Fort Pitt withstood the onslaught of a great Indian uprising lead by Pontiac. All other fortified posts on the upper Ohio and the Great Lakes were taken by surprise and treachery. At Detroit Major Gladwin was warned by an unknown informant—no one knows exactly where the warning came from—and the fort withstood a long siege until relieved with great difficulty by a force led by Colonel John Montresor (whose portrait by Copley hangs in Gallery 28). Stanley, a Detroit painter, illustrates the popular legend that Gladwin was warned by a beautiful Indian girl who loved him, as it is told in Parkman's "Conspiracy of Pontiac." Dated 1863.

works.title: Naval Engagement Between the "United States" and the "Macedonian"
works.lender: Lent by The Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia.
works.note: The "United States" commanded by Decatur captured the "Macedonian," forty-nine guns, on October 25, 1812. The exploits of the tiny United States navy at sea and the battles of Plattsburg, Niagara and New Orleans (see Andrew Jackson) relieved the otherwise inglorious War of 1812 and made a great appeal to the popular imagination. Thomas Birch had been a portrait and landscape painter in Philadelphia until he was inspired by the naval battles of 1812 to paint a series of these gallant naval engagements. Dated painted in 1813.

works.title: The Verdict of the People
works.lender: Lent by The Boatmen's National Bank of St. Louis, Missouri.
works.note: The rise of political party organization and party loyalties was not foreseen in our plan of government as it was originally conceived by its founders. The national political parties of today are a creation of the early nineteenth century. Bingham, a Missouri artist, was very actively interested in politics before painting this election scene. In 1848 he had been elected to the state legislature and in 1852 had been a delegate to the national Whig convention. He thus had first hand experience of the turbulent elections of those days when party loyalties were intense and the secret ballot unheard of. This picture was intended by the artist to be the climax of a series of paintings of election scenes and he wrote of it, "I intend it to be a representation of the scene that takes place at the close of an exciting political contest, just when the final result of the ballot is proclaimed from the stand of the judges. The subject will doubtless strike you as one well calculated to furnish that contrast and variety of expression which confers the chief value upon pictures of this class." Dated 1855.

works.title: Prisoners from the Front
works.lender: Lent by The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York City.
works.note:
The national consciousness created by the first seventy years of the republic was put to its greatest test in the Civil War, 1861-65, when the interests of one region came into violent clash with the love of the Union. The instinct for unity won and decided that the vast new continent with all its diverse regions should be one country and one people. To foreigners the diversity of race and geography in the United States is so great that they wonder what holds it together—and, like Hitler, think it will easily fall apart under pressure. They do not remember that we fought and won a four year war as bitter, bloody and costly as any of modern times with the watchword, the Union must and shall be preserved.

Winslow Homer was attached for a time as war illustrator to the 61st New York volunteers, whose colonel Francis C. Barlow, is represented here interviewing prisoners. Homer represents the American soldier as we, too, know him—not a professional fighter but a civilian by instinct who does his dangerous and comfortless job well because it is his duty. Dated 1866.
works.label: Detroit Institute of Arts 1944–45

works.title: Defiance — Inviting a Shot Before Petersburg, Virginia
works.lender: Lent by the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York City.
works.note: By the summer of 1864 the southern cause was lost but the magnificent Army of Northern Virginia fought on for a year longer in defense of the southern capitol. The nine months siege of Petersburg, which guarded the approach to Richmond from the south, lasted through the winter of 1864-65. Homer here depicts one of the incidents of the trench warfare with the keen observation, austere simplicity of form and sober force of feeling which characterize all of his work. Dated 1864.
works.label: Detroit Institute of Arts 1944–45

works.title: The Veteran
works.lender: Lent by Miss Adelaide Milton de Groot, by courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York City.
works.note: This canvas painted in 1865 represents the emotions with which one great American artist saw the end of the Civil War. The sober power of his image of the returned veteran swinging his scythe in the harvest field, the originality of his approach and absence of sentimentality, give great dignity to his expression of an emotion which we all can understand today. Dated 1865.

works.title: The Italian Shepherd Boy
works.note: The impression Allston's reveries made upon the sensitive minds of his time may be realized from what Margaret Fuller later wrote about her first meeting with his pictures. "The calm and meditative cast of these pictures, the ideal beauty that shone through rather than in them, and the harmony of coloring were as unlike anything else I saw, as the Vicar of Wakefield to Cooper's novels. I seemed to recognize in painting that self-possessed elegance, that transparent depth, which I most admired in literature; I thought with delight that such a man as this had been able to grow up in our bustling, reasonable community, that he had kept his foot upon the ground, yet never lost sight of the rose-clouds of beauty floating above him. I saw too that he had not been troubled, but possessed his own soul with the blandest patience, and I hoped, I scarce know what, probably the mot d'enigme for which we are all looking. How the poetical mind can live and work in peace and good faith! how it may unfold to its due perfection in an unpoetical society!" Dated 1819.
works.label: Detroit Institute of Arts 1944–45

works.title: The Court of Death
works.note:
A hopeful movement toward mural painting of patriotic themes sprang up after the successful close of the War of 1812, but soon died out for lack of opportunity. Few public buildings offered wall space for murals and still fewer public bodies were ready to patronize the arts. The enthusiasm for large pictures then took a curious twist—artists painted huge pictures for the purpose of carrying them about the country, exhibiting them in hired halls and charging admission. The most famous and the most successful of these exhibition pictures was The Court of Death, painted by Rembrandt Peale in 1820. According to Peale's own statement, he took in $8886.00 in a little over a year from exhibiting this picture.

The idea was suggested by a passage in a poem on Death by Bishop Porteus. The elaborate allegory is as follows:

Death sits in the center, his foot on the corpse of a man in the prime of life, to illustrate his power over mankind. The head and feet of the corpse touch the waters of oblivion, to indicate the mystery surrounding the origin and end of life.

On either side of Death are his principal agents. On the right, War, Conflagration, Famine and Pestilence, rush over the fallen warrior and the widow and orphan.

On the left are Pleasure, who presents the cup to Intemperance, behind whom Remorse covers his face with his hands. Next are Delirium Tremens and Suicide. Beyond are a group of Consumption, Despair, Fever, Apoplexy, Hypochondria and Gout.

In front Old Age, supported by Faith, resigned but unterrified greets the figure of Death. Dated 1820.
works.label: Detroit Institute of Arts 1944–45

works.title: The Voyage of Life — Youth
works.lender: Lent by St. Luke's Hospital, New York City.
works.note: The series of four paintings called the Voyage of Life were commissioned by the New York banker Samuel Ward, the father of "Uncle Sam" Ward and of Julia Ward Howe. It depicts first childhood, with the soul watched over by the good angel; youth (the present one) led astray by hope and pleasure; manhood, surrounded by storms and all the demons of destruction; and finally as old age enters the ocean of eternity in his shattered bark, his oars of self-reliance broken, helpless and repentant, the good angel returns once more to direct his gaze upward to heaven. The painting of pairs or series of compositions to tell a story of this kind, popularized by Cole, was very characteristic of romantic taste. The narrative element in painting, which produced the great fresco cycles of the Middle Ages and Renaissance, has never been fully acclimatized in American art. The first movement of romantic narrative painting (see Peale's Court of Death) was spent when Cole gave the impulse a different form and subject matter, which made it better suited to the taste and patronage of private individuals. In spite of its sentimentality The Voyage of Life reflects accurately the strongly ethical tone of American thought at that time. The exhibition of The Voyage of Life in Boston and New York with the artist's printed explanations caused a great sensation, comparable to the Armory Show of 1913 or the Rivera Frescoes in 1932. Dated 1840.

works.title: Wolfert's Will
works.lender: Lent by The Brooklyn Museum, Brooklyn.
works.note:
The illustration of subjects from romantic literature was less characteristic of American romantic painting than of European. But the genial humor and fantasy of Washington Irving's tales were the main inspiration of John Quidor. This is the last scene from "Wolfert Webber or Golden Dreams" in Tales of a Traveler. Wolfert was one of the placid Knickerbocker Dutch who were Irving's best comic characters. After terrifying and heartbreaking adventures while trying to find a pirate's buried treasure, Wolfert returned broken-hearted to die in poverty (as he supposed) on his ancestral cabbage farm in Manhattan:

He begged the lawyer to be brief, for he felt his end approaching and that he had no time to lose. The lawyer nibbed his pen, spread out his paper, and prepared to write. "I give and bequeath," said Wolfert faintly, "my small farm—"

"What—all" exclaimed the lawyer.

"Yes—all," said he.

"What! all that great patch of land with cabbages and sunflowers, which the corporation is just going to run a main street through?"

"The same," said Wolfert, with a heavy sigh, and sinking back upon his pillow.

"I wish him joy that inherits it!" said the little lawyer chuckling and rubbing his hands involuntarily.

"What do you mean?" said Wolfert, again opening his eyes.

"That he'll be one of the richest men in the place!" cried little Rollebuck.

The expiring Wolfert seemed to step back from the threshold of existence: his eyes again lighted up; he raised himself in his bed, shoved back his worsted red night cap, and stared broadly at the lawyer.

"You don't say so!" exclaimed he . . . "why, then I think I'll not make my will yet!" Dated 1856.
